description_full: Kilroy Realty Corporation is a leading U.S. landlord and developer, with operations in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Seattle, San Diego, and Austin. The Company has earned global recognition for sustainability, building operations, innovation, and design. As a pioneer and innovator in the creation of a more sustainable real estate industry, the Company's approach to modern business environments helps drive creativity and productivity for some of the world's leading technology, media, life science, and professional services companies. The Company is a publicly traded real estate investment trust (REIT) and member of the S&P MidCap 400 Index with more than seven decades of experience managing, developing, and acquiring office, life science, and mixed-use projects. As of June 30, 2026, Kilroy's stabilized portfolio totaled approximately 17.1 million square feet of primarily office and life science space that was 77.0% occupied and 81.5% leased. The Company also has 608 residential units in San Diego, with a quarterly average occupancy of 95.6%. Kilroy Realty Corporation was incorporated in 1947 in Maryland. Kilroy Realty Corporation is based in Los Angeles, California.
ceo_bio: Ms. Angela M. Aman | CEO & Director | Age 46 | Compensation: $2.6M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 241 people. Revenue per employee of $4.6M ranks in the above the sector median among Real Estate peers, improving at 9%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $1.9M of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $79K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Kilroy Realty Corporation is a mid-cap real estate business with a $4.2B market cap on $1.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +0% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 17% against a 10% cost of capital, a 8-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $450M in free cash flow — roughly 40 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.05× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 2.5× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 6.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 15% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 18% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 30% and a beta of 1.02, it moves roughly with the market.
About $45.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 44% in the 2020 crash, 50% in the 2022 bear market and 71% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 11% below its DCF fair value of $40.27, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $32.70 to $50.46 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Real Estate peers: cheaper on P/FCF 9.3 vs 17.8, richer on P/E 143.3 vs 23.6 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 10.7% (above the risk-free rate).
The 14 covering analysts target $39.71 on average, 11% above the price.
The price implies 6.9% annual cash-flow growth, 2pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 17% clears the cost of capital of 9.8% by 8pp, the mark of a value creator.
It converts 40% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.05x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 40%.
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.0x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.7% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.60 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 0.5% over 3 years, 4.4% over 5 years and 6.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Free cash flow has compounded 6.7% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 4.4% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (10.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 43, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 19.2% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.9%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $2.6M sold).
It returns 6.1% a year to shareholders (6.0% in dividends).
It pays out 864% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 15.2% of the float, 8.5 days to cover.
people: With about 241 employees, each generates about $4.6M of revenue, 2.0x the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 9.1% a year.
That works out to $1.9M of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.6M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
